1.1 LeetCode#

1.1.1 No two adjacent equal items (LeetCode 767) and the cooldown version (LeetCode 621)#

Asked: PhD new grad (1124594), level not stated (1125433, 1124873, 1057160, 1050390, 1123499)

Question.

  • Given a list of games, return a reordering in which the same game never appears twice in a row (1124594).
  • Counts form (1125433): the input maps each item to its number of copies. Part 1: decide whether all copies fit in one row with no two equal neighbours, then rewrite that check as short as possible. Part 2: build such a row; after a heap answer, the follow-up was to reach O(N)O(N)O(N).
  • LeetCode 767 (Reorganize String) itself (1057160, 1124873, 1123499), also split into "is it feasible?" and "output any valid string" (1050390). In a complexity follow-up the interviewer did not accept O(N)O(N)O(N) and wanted the kkk distinct items counted, O(N+k)O(N+k)O(N+k) (1123499).
  • Cooldown version, LeetCode 621 (Task Scheduler), posed as an "Experience Scheduler" (1123499): two equal tasks need at least nnn slots between them and idle slots are allowed; return the fewest slots.

Answer. Drop zero counts, then let NNN be the number of items, k≤Nk\le Nk≤N the number of distinct items, cic_ici​ their counts and m=max⁡icim=\max_i c_im=maxi​ci​. The mmm copies of the top item need m−1m-1m−1 separators, so

feasible  ⟺  N−m≥m−1  ⟺  m≤⌈N2⌉=⌊N+12⌋.\text{feasible} \iff N-m \ge m-1 \iff m \le \left\lceil \tfrac{N}{2} \right\rceil = \left\lfloor \tfrac{N+1}{2} \right\rfloor .feasible⟺N−m≥m−1⟺m≤⌈2N​⌉=⌊2N+1​⌋.

The floor form is the one-line check, with no odd/even split. Linear construction: write the top item on slots 0,2,4,…0,2,4,\dots0,2,4,…, continue with the other items in any order on the remaining even slots, then wrap to 1,3,5,…1,3,5,\dots1,3,5,…. Only a block that wraps from the even to the odd slots can touch itself, and that needs c≥⌈N/2⌉c \ge \lceil N/2\rceilc≥⌈N/2⌉ copies. The top item has m≤⌈N/2⌉m \le \lceil N/2\rceilm≤⌈N/2⌉, so it never wraps; any later item that wraps starts at the aaa-th even slot with a≥ma \ge ma≥m, so c≤m≤a<⌈N/2⌉c \le m \le a < \lceil N/2\rceilc≤m≤a<⌈N/2⌉. Cost: O(N+k)=O(N)O(N+k)=O(N)O(N+k)=O(N) time because k≤Nk\le Nk≤N, so both answers to the complexity follow-up describe the same bound; O(k)O(k)O(k) space plus the output. Only the top item has to go first, which is what removes the sort and the heap; the heap greedy (always place the most frequent item that differs from the previous one) costs O(Nlog⁡k)O(N\log k)O(Nlogk). When no arrangement exists, return an empty list (LeetCode 767 itself returns ""). Edge cases: N≤1N\le 1N≤1; a single distinct item with c>1c>1c>1; zero counts in the map; odd NNN with m=(N+1)/2m=(N+1)/2m=(N+1)/2, which forces the top item onto every even slot.

For LeetCode 621, with ttt the number of tasks tied at count mmm:

Tmin⁡=max⁡(N, (m−1)(n+1)+t).T_{\min} = \max\bigl(N,\ (m-1)(n+1)+t\bigr).Tmin​=max(N, (m−1)(n+1)+t).

The top tasks open m−1m-1m−1 frames of n+1n+1n+1 slots plus a last frame of ttt slots; the other tasks fill the gaps, and if they overflow the frames no idle slot is needed, so the answer is NNN. O(N)O(N)O(N) time and O(k)O(k)O(k) space; a heap simulation of (n+1)(n+1)(n+1)-slot cycles also works in O(Tlog⁡k)O(T\log k)O(Tlogk) for TTT output slots. With n=1n=1n=1, Tmin⁡=NT_{\min}=NTmin​=N exactly when the LeetCode 767 test passes.

Coding: no two adjacent equal items, and LeetCode 621 [READY]View exercise
python
from collections import Counter


def can_arrange(counts):
    """counts maps item -> copies. True if every copy fits in one row with no equal neighbours."""
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return max(counts.values(), default=0) <= (total + 1) // 2


def arrange_no_adjacent(items):
    """Reorder items so that no two neighbours are equal; [] if that is impossible."""
    counts = Counter(items)
    if not can_arrange(counts):
        return []
    top = max(counts, key=counts.get, default=None)
    order = [top] + [item for item in counts if item != top]   # only the most frequent must go first
    result = [None] * len(items)
    slot = 0
    for item in order:
        for _ in range(counts[item]):
            result[slot] = item
            slot += 2                       # even slots first, then odd slots
            if slot >= len(items):
                slot = 1
    return result


def least_interval(tasks, n):
    """LeetCode 621: fewest time slots when equal tasks must be at least n slots apart."""
    counts = Counter(tasks)
    top = max(counts.values(), default=0)
    tied = sum(1 for c in counts.values() if c == top)
    return max(len(tasks), (top - 1) * (n + 1) + tied)

Time complexity: can_arrange is O(k)O(k)O(k) for kkk distinct items; arrange_no_adjacent is O(N)O(N)O(N): one count, one pass over the slots; least_interval is O(N)O(N)O(N).

Space complexity: O(k)O(k)O(k) for the counts, plus the O(N)O(N)O(N) output.

Only the most frequent item has to go first; the other items can fill the remaining slots in any order. That is what removes the sort and the heap.

1.1.2 Sliding-window rate limiter, then per key#

Asked: new grad (1156803)

Question. Implement a sliding-window rate limiter that decides, request by request, whether a timestamped request is allowed under a cap of KKK requests per window of length WWW; the thread points to LeetCode 362 (Design Hit Counter) as the same shape and solves it with a deque. Follow-up: apply the limit separately per key, which the thread solves with a dict from key to deque.

Answer. Assume non-decreasing timestamps and keep a deque of accepted timestamps. For a request at time ttt, pop from the left while the oldest entry is ≤t−W\le t-W≤t−W, so the window is (t−W,t](t-W,t](t−W,t]; accept if fewer than KKK entries remain, and append ttt only on accept, so denied requests never count. Per key, keep a dict from key to deque. If there are two caps, for example one per user and one per experience (a Roblox game), evict expired entries in both deques, accept only if both are under their caps, then append to both; recording the request in one deque when the other denies it would spend the user's budget on a rejected request. Each accepted timestamp is pushed and popped at most once per deque, so a request costs amortised O(1)O(1)O(1) per cap, and memory is O(K)O(K)O(K) per key seen. A deque is trimmed only when its own key sends a request, so idle keys keep stale entries: sweep periodically and delete the deques that become empty. Clarify whether the window is (t−W,t](t-W,t](t−W,t] or [t−W,t][t-W,t][t−W,t], whether denied requests count, whether timestamps can arrive out of order (then use buckets or a sorted structure), and what K=0K=0K=0 means. Alternatives to name: a fixed-window counter is cheaper but admits up to 2K2K2K requests across a window boundary; a sliding-window counter interpolates two fixed windows; a token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity; LeetCode 362 keeps a ring of WWW one-second buckets.

Coding: sliding-window rate limiter, per key and with two caps [READY]View exercise
python
from collections import defaultdict, deque


class SlidingWindowRateLimiter:
    """At most max_requests per key in any window (t - window, t]. Rejected requests are not stored.
    Timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order."""

    def __init__(self, max_requests, window):
        self.max_requests, self.window = max_requests, window
        self.accepted = defaultdict(deque)        # key -> timestamps of accepted requests

    def allow(self, key, timestamp):
        recent = self.accepted[key]
        while recent and recent[0] <= timestamp - self.window:
            recent.popleft()                      # fell out of the window
        if len(recent) < self.max_requests:
            recent.append(timestamp)
            return True
        return False


class MultiCapRateLimiter:
    """Follow-up: one cap per dimension, e.g. limits = {"user": 3, "experience": 5}.
    allow(t, user="u1", experience="g7") accepts only if every dimension is under its cap."""

    def __init__(self, limits, window):
        self.limits, self.window = limits, window
        self.accepted = {dim: defaultdict(deque) for dim in limits}

    def allow(self, timestamp, **keys):
        queues = [(self.accepted[dim][keys[dim]], cap) for dim, cap in self.limits.items()]
        for recent, _ in queues:
            while recent and recent[0] <= timestamp - self.window:
                recent.popleft()
        if any(len(recent) >= cap for recent, cap in queues):
            return False                          # record nothing when any cap denies
        for recent, _ in queues:
            recent.append(timestamp)
        return True

Time complexity: amortised O(1)O(1)O(1) per request and dimension: every accepted timestamp is appended once and popped at most once.

Space complexity: O(K)O(K)O(K) timestamps per key and dimension, for a cap of KKK, for every key seen so far. A deque is trimmed only when its own key sends a request, so an idle key keeps up to KKK stale timestamps and is never removed. To forget idle keys, sweep periodically (or keep keys in last-seen order), evict expired timestamps and delete the deques that become empty.

The two-cap version checks every dimension before it records anything, so a request denied by the experience cap does not use up the user's budget.

1.1.3 Valid Parentheses, extended step by step#

Asked: intern (1063311)

Question. A medium-level extension of Valid Parentheses (LeetCode 20), apparently written by the interviewer, asked one step at a time. The individual steps were not reported.

Answer. Work through the standard ladder; every rung except the last is one linear pass.

  • Several bracket types (LeetCode 20): push openers; on a closer, pop and compare with its opener, failing if the stack is empty; the string is valid if and only if the stack is empty at the end. O(n)O(n)O(n) time and space.
  • Fewest insertions to make it valid (LeetCode 921): count unmatched ( as open; a ) with open at 0 costs one insertion, otherwise it decrements open; the answer is the insertions plus the final open. O(1)O(1)O(1) space.
  • Fewest removals, returning the string (LeetCode 1249): collect the indices of unmatched ( on a stack and of unmatched ) as they occur, then rebuild the string skipping both. O(n)O(n)O(n).
  • Longest valid substring (LeetCode 32): a stack of indices seeded with −1-1−1; on ( push iii; on ) pop, then push iii if the stack is empty, else the candidate length is i−topi-\text{top}i−top. Two counter passes, left to right and right to left, do it in O(1)O(1)O(1) space.
  • * may be (, ) or empty (LeetCode 678): track the range [lo,hi][lo,hi][lo,hi] of possible open counts; ( adds 1 to both ends, ) subtracts 1 from both, * moves lololo down and hihihi up by 1; fail if hi<0hi<0hi<0, clamp lololo at 0, and accept if lo=0lo=0lo=0 at the end. O(1)O(1)O(1) space.
  • Generate every valid string with nnn pairs (LeetCode 22): backtrack under close≤open≤n\text{close}\le\text{open}\le nclose≤open≤n; the output has Cn=1n+1(2nn)C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}Cn​=n+11​(n2n​) strings.

Edge cases: the empty string is valid; ask whether characters other than brackets are ignored or rejected.

1.1.4 Remove prefixes from an array#

Asked: research intern (1047347)

Question. Remove prefixes from an array: give a brute force, analyse its complexity, then optimise, with a trie as the hinted direction. The input and output format was not given; the reading that fits the trie hint is a list of strings from which every string that is a prefix of another string is removed.

Answer. Let nnn be the number of words, LLL their total length and ℓ\ellℓ the longest length. The brute force runs a prefix check on every ordered pair, O(n2ℓ)O(n^2\ell)O(n2ℓ); bucketing by first letter does not change the worst case. Trie: insert every word and count the words ending at each node; a word is a proper prefix of another word exactly when its end node has a child (or when its end count is above 1, if a duplicate counts as "another string"); keep the remaining words in input order. O(L)O(L)O(L) time and O(L)O(L)O(L) nodes. If the task is the other way round (drop every word that has another word as a prefix), drop a word when its path passes through another word's end node, in the same O(L)O(L)O(L). Sort: after a lexicographic sort, the strings that start with sss form one contiguous block beginning with sss, so sss is a proper prefix of some word exactly when the next string that differs from sss starts with sss; O(ℓ nlog⁡n)O(\ell\, n\log n)O(ℓnlogn). Clarify duplicates, the empty string (a prefix of every word), case sensitivity, and whether the task is instead to strip the longest common prefix from every string (LeetCode 14, O(L)O(L)O(L)).

1.1.5 Most frequent call path from function-call logs#

Asked: senior (1186156), staff (1136387)

Question. The input is a list of trace lines: -> f means f is called and <- f means f returns. Parse the lines and return the call stack, written from the root as main->eventClick->eventClickAction, that occurs most often. On ["-> main", "-> eventClick", "-> eventClickAction", "<- eventClickAction", "-> eventClickAction", "<- eventClickAction", "<- eventClick", "<- main"] the answer is main->eventClick->eventClickAction with frequency 2, formed once by lines 1-3 and again by lines 1, 2 and 5. Follow-ups: also return the count (1136387); the logs come from several threads, interleaved (1186156).

Answer. Replay the log with a stack. On a call, push the name and add 1 to the counter of the current root-to-top path; on a return, check that the name matches the top and pop, and raise an error for a return that does not match or arrives on an empty stack. Keying the counter by the joined stack costs O(D)O(D)O(D) per line, so O(E⋅D)O(E\cdot D)O(E⋅D) for EEE lines and maximum depth DDD. To get O(E)O(E)O(E), give each distinct path a node id in a call tree: map (parent_id, name) to the child's id with one hash lookup, keep node ids on the stack, so a call is one lookup plus one increment, and rebuild only the winning path through parent pointers in O(D)O(D)O(D); space is O(P)O(P)O(P) for PPP distinct paths. Track the best path as you go, ranked by (count, depth) with a strict comparison: counts only grow, so the running best is the final best, ties go to the deeper path, and among equal ranks the path that reached the count first wins (state this tie rule, since none was given). For interleaved threads, keep a dict from thread id to that thread's stack and share one counter, so equal paths merge across threads (confirm that this is wanted, and ask how a line names its thread); the complexity is unchanged. Recursion, a name repeating inside a path, needs no special case. Counting at the call already counts calls still open at the end; ask whether a stack that is a prefix of a longer one counts, since counting only leaf stacks gives different answers in general.

Coding: most frequent call path, single and multi-threaded [READY]View exercise
python
def most_frequent_call_path(traces):
    """traces: '-> f' is a call, '<- f' a return. Every call counts the stack root -> f once.
    Returns (path, count); ties go to the deeper path, then to the path that reached the count first."""
    stack, counts = [], {}
    best, best_key = None, (0, 0)
    for line in traces:
        arrow, name = line.split()
        if arrow == '->':
            stack.append(name)
            path = '->'.join(stack)
            counts[path] = counts.get(path, 0) + 1
            key = (counts[path], len(stack))
            if key > best_key:              # strict: an equal key keeps the earlier path
                best, best_key = path, key
        elif arrow == '<-' and stack and stack[-1] == name:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            raise ValueError(f'unmatched trace line: {line!r}')
    return best, best_key[0]


def most_frequent_call_path_threads(logs):
    """Follow-up: lines are '<thread> -> f' or '<thread> <- f', interleaved across threads.
    One stack per thread; paths are counted across all threads."""
    stacks, counts = {}, {}
    best, best_key = None, (0, 0)
    for line in logs:
        thread, arrow, name = line.split()
        stack = stacks.setdefault(thread, [])
        if arrow == '->':
            stack.append(name)
            path = '->'.join(stack)
            counts[path] = counts.get(path, 0) + 1
            key = (counts[path], len(stack))
            if key > best_key:
                best, best_key = path, key
        elif arrow == '<-' and stack and stack[-1] == name:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            raise ValueError(f'unmatched trace line: {line!r}')
    return best, best_key[0]

Time complexity: O(E⋅D)O(E \cdot D)O(E⋅D) for EEE trace lines and stack depth DDD, because each call joins the current stack into a key. Keying the counter by call-tree node ids, as in the sketch above, makes it O(E)O(E)O(E).

Space complexity: O(P⋅D)O(P \cdot D)O(P⋅D) for PPP distinct paths stored as strings, plus one stack per thread.

The input format of the multi-threaded logs was not reported; this version assumes each line starts with a thread id, such as t1 -> main. Ask before you parse.

1.1.6 Match-3 grid (Candy Crush)#

Asked: senior (1147380), level not stated (1150441, 886138)

Question. The input is a grid of integers, and a horizontal or vertical run of 3 or more equal values is a match. Part 1: output every match as (value, length), listing all matches of one direction before the other (the poster recalls vertical first but is unsure), scanning left to right and top to bottom; a reader saw a version that outputs (position, length) instead. Part 2: set every matched cell to 0 and let the cells above fall into the gaps (1147380). LeetCode 723 (Candy Crush) as written: crush, drop, and repeat until the board is stable (1150441). The third thread names the match-3 problem without details (886138).

Answer. Part 1: scan each column, then each row, for maximal runs with two pointers; a run [j,k)[j,k)[j,k) of equal non-zero values with k−j≥3k-j\ge 3k−j≥3 is one match. Report each as (value, length, start cell, direction), which covers both output formats, with vertical runs first. O(RC)O(RC)O(RC) time. A run of 5 is one match of length 5, not three overlapping triples, and an L or T shape gives two matches that share a cell. Part 2: mark every matched cell first and clear afterwards, because clearing during the scan breaks crossing runs; then, per column, move a write pointer up from the bottom, copy non-zero cells down to it and fill the top with 0, in O(RC)O(RC)O(RC). LeetCode 723: repeat detect, clear and drop while any match exists. Every productive pass turns at least 3 non-zero cells into 0 and gravity creates none, so there are at most ⌊RC/3⌋+1\lfloor RC/3\rfloor+1⌊RC/3⌋+1 passes and O((RC)2)O\bigl((RC)^2\bigr)O((RC)2) time in the worst case. 0 means empty and never matches; on a rectangular board keep the row and column bounds straight.

Coding: match-3 runs, clear and drop, Candy Crush [READY]View exercise
python
def find_matches(board):
    """Runs of 3+ equal non-zero values. Vertical runs first (columns left to right, top to bottom),
    then horizontal runs (rows top to bottom, left to right). Each run: (value, length, (row, col), direction)."""
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0]) if board else 0
    runs = []
    for c in range(cols):
        r = 0
        while r < rows:
            end = r
            while end + 1 < rows and board[end + 1][c] == board[r][c]:
                end += 1
            if board[r][c] and end - r + 1 >= 3:
                runs.append((board[r][c], end - r + 1, (r, c), 'V'))
            r = end + 1
    for r in range(rows):
        c = 0
        while c < cols:
            end = c
            while end + 1 < cols and board[r][end + 1] == board[r][c]:
                end += 1
            if board[r][c] and end - c + 1 >= 3:
                runs.append((board[r][c], end - c + 1, (r, c), 'H'))
            c = end + 1
    return runs


def crush_once(board):
    """Phase 2: set every matched cell to 0, then let the non-zero cells fall. Returns whether anything matched."""
    runs = find_matches(board)
    for _, length, (r, c), direction in runs:
        for k in range(length):
            if direction == 'V':
                board[r + k][c] = 0
            else:
                board[r][c + k] = 0
    for c in range(len(board[0]) if board else 0):
        column = [board[r][c] for r in range(len(board)) if board[r][c]]
        column = [0] * (len(board) - len(column)) + column
        for r in range(len(board)):
            board[r][c] = column[r]
    return bool(runs)


def candy_crush(board):
    """LeetCode 723: crush and drop until the board is stable."""
    while crush_once(board):
        pass
    return board

Time complexity: O(RC)O(RC)O(RC) for find_matches and for crush_once; candy_crush calls crush_once at most ⌊RC/3⌋+1\lfloor RC/3\rfloor + 1⌊RC/3⌋+1 times, because every call that matches turns at least 3 non-zero cells into 0, gravity never creates a non-zero cell, and the last call finds nothing; so O((RC)2)O((RC)^2)O((RC)2) in the worst case.

Space complexity: find_matches uses O(1)O(1)O(1) besides its output list, which can hold at most 2RC/32RC/32RC/3 runs. crush_once adds an O(R)O(R)O(R) column buffer for the drop and builds that run list internally, so its extra space is O(RC)O(RC)O(RC) in the worst case. The board is changed in place.

Vertical runs are listed before horizontal ones because that is the order the report remembers; the poster was not sure, so confirm it. Each run is reported as value, length, start cell and direction, which covers both reported output formats.

1.1.7 Sliding windows that contain a target#

Asked: senior (1177250), level not stated (1173576)

Question. Given a list of numbers, a fixed window size www and a target: part 1, return every window of size www that contains the target; part 2, return the first window in which the target appears the most times (1173576). The other thread gives part 1 only, as "given windows and a target number, return the windows that contain it" (1177250).

Answer. The windows start at i=0,…,n−wi=0,\dots,n-wi=0,…,n−w. Slide a count of the target:

cnti+1=cnti−[xi=t]+[xi+w=t].\mathrm{cnt}_{i+1} = \mathrm{cnt}_i - [x_i = t] + [x_{i+w} = t].cnti+1​=cnti​−[xi​=t]+[xi+w​=t].

Part 1 returns every window with cnti>0\mathrm{cnt}_i>0cnti​>0. Part 2 takes the argmax with a strict comparison, so the earliest window wins ties, and returns nothing (None) when no window contains the target. Sliding is O(n)O(n)O(n) time and O(1)O(1)O(1) extra space; returning copies of the windows costs O(w)O(w)O(w) each, so part 1 is O(nw)O(nw)O(nw) in the worst case and part 2 is O(n+w)O(n+w)O(n+w). Return start indices instead if positions are enough. Edge cases: require w≥1w\ge 1w≥1; w>nw>nw>n or an empty list gives no window, w=nw=nw=n gives exactly one, and the last start is n−wn-wn−w. If the windows arrive as a given list, part 1 is a plain scan of each window.

Coding: windows that contain a target [READY]View exercise
python
def windows_with_target(nums, k, target):
    """Every length-k window (in order) that contains target. One pass keeps the target count of the window."""
    windows, count = [], 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        count += x == target
        if i >= k:
            count -= nums[i - k] == target       # the element that just left the window
        if i >= k - 1 and count:
            windows.append(nums[i - k + 1:i + 1])
    return windows


def first_window_with_most_target(nums, k, target):
    """The earliest length-k window with the most copies of target; None if no window contains it."""
    best_start, best, count = None, 0, 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        count += x == target
        if i >= k:
            count -= nums[i - k] == target
        if i >= k - 1 and count > best:          # strict: ties keep the earlier window
            best, best_start = count, i - k + 1
    return None if best_start is None else nums[best_start:best_start + k]

Time complexity: O(n)O(n)O(n) to slide the count, plus O(k)O(k)O(k) to copy each returned window (kkk is the window size, www in the sketch). Part 1 is therefore O(nk)O(nk)O(nk) in the worst case, when almost every window contains the target; part 2 copies one window, so O(n+k)O(n+k)O(n+k).

Space complexity: O(1)O(1)O(1) besides the returned windows.

Return start indices instead of copies if the interviewer only needs positions.

1.1.8 Find median from a data stream (LeetCode 295)#

Asked: IC6 (principal) (995525), level not stated (1014514)

Question. LeetCode 295: support adding numbers from a stream and returning the median of all numbers so far. Follow-ups: multiple data streams, and reservoir sampling (1014514).

Answer. Use two heaps: a max-heap lo with the smaller half and a min-heap hi with the larger half, kept so that max⁡(lo)≤min⁡(hi)\max(lo)\le\min(hi)max(lo)≤min(hi) and ∣lo∣−∣hi∣∈{0,1}|lo|-|hi|\in\{0,1\}∣lo∣−∣hi∣∈{0,1}. To add, push into lo, move the top of lo to hi, and move the top of hi back if hi became larger. The median is the top of lo for an odd count and the mean of both tops for an even count; querying an empty stream is an error. O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) per add, O(1)O(1)O(1) per query, O(n)O(n)O(n) space. Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated values in lo, and return a float in the even case.

Multiple streams: for one global median, feed every stream into the same structure; for a median per stream, keep a dict from stream id to its own heap pair; for integer values in a bounded range of size VVV, a Fenwick tree over value counts finds the kkk-th smallest in O(log⁡V)O(\log V)O(logV) and merges streams by adding counts in O(V)O(V)O(V); a median over the last www items is LeetCode 480, two heaps with lazy deletion.

Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R) keeps a uniform sample of kkk items in O(k)O(k)O(k) memory: keep the first kkk; for item i>ki>ki>k, draw jjj uniformly from {1,…,i}\{1,\dots,i\}{1,…,i} and replace slot jjj if j≤kj\le kj≤k. Item i>ki>ki>k is in the final sample with probability

ki∏j=i+1n(1−1j)=ki⋅in=kn,\frac{k}{i}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{j}\Bigr) = \frac{k}{i}\cdot\frac{i}{n} = \frac{k}{n},ik​j=i+1∏n​(1−j1​)=ik​⋅ni​=nk​,

and each of the first kkk items with ∏j=k+1n(1−1/j)=k/n\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(1-1/j)=k/n∏j=k+1n​(1−1/j)=k/n. The sample median then estimates the stream median. For a guaranteed rank error of εn\varepsilon nεn, use a GK sketch (deterministic) or a KLL sketch (with high probability); t-digest is accurate in practice but has no worst-case bound.

Coding: median of a data stream with two heaps [READY]View exercise
python
import heapq


class MedianFinder:
    """LeetCode 295. low holds the smaller half as a max-heap (negated), high the larger half."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.low, self.high = [], []

    def add_num(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.low, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.high, -heapq.heappop(self.low))   # the largest of low moves to high
        if len(self.high) > len(self.low):
            heapq.heappush(self.low, -heapq.heappop(self.high))

    def find_median(self):
        if not self.low:
            raise ValueError('no numbers yet')
        if len(self.low) > len(self.high):
            return float(-self.low[0])
        return (-self.low[0] + self.high[0]) / 2

Time complexity: O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) per add_num, O(1)O(1)O(1) per find_median.

Space complexity: O(n)O(n)O(n) for the two heaps.

1.1.9 Word search on a board (LeetCode 79 / 212)#

Asked: level not stated (919123, 832731)

Question. Given char[][] board and string[] words: (1) return the words that can be formed on the board; (2) also return a path for each such word; (3) different words may not reuse a board cell, so return the largest set of words that fit together (919123). A second ladder (832731): (1) decide whether a given character appears in any of the four directions from a coordinate; (2) LeetCode 79, decide whether one word is in the grid; (3) decide which of many words are in the grid, approach only (a trie of the words).

Answer. LeetCode 79: DFS from every cell along 4-neighbour steps, marking a cell used on the way in and freeing it on the way out; O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1)O(RC\cdot 4\cdot 3^{L-1})O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1) for a word of length LLL. Many words (LeetCode 212): build a trie of the words and run one DFS per start cell that follows trie edges, so shared prefixes are walked once; record each word the first time its end is reached, and prune trie leaves that become empty. Building the trie is O(Ltotal)O(L_{\text{total}})O(Ltotal​) and the search is O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1)O(RC\cdot 4\cdot 3^{L-1})O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1) for the longest word length LLL. Paths come for free: the DFS stack is the path, copied when a word ends.

Disjoint cells need every candidate path of each word, not the one path per word kept above. On the one-row board a b a b with words ab and ba, a row-major search keeps ab on (0,0),(0,1)(0,0),(0,1)(0,0),(0,1) and a path for ba that starts at (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), so the two overlap, yet ba also fits on (0,3),(0,2)(0,3),(0,2)(0,3),(0,2). So collect all candidate paths per word, then backtrack: for each word either skip it or take one of its paths that avoids the cells already used, pruning when the current size plus the words left cannot beat the best. This is set packing and exponential in general, so it suits small boards. For the single-character question, ask whether "four directions" means the four neighbours, O(1)O(1)O(1), or the four straight rays, O(R+C)O(R+C)O(R+C). Clarify 4 or 8 directions, whether a word may reuse a cell, and case sensitivity.

Coding: word search on a board with a trie, with paths [READY]View exercise
python
def find_words(board, words):
    """LeetCode 212 with the paths follow-up: map each word that can be traced on the board
    (4-neighbour steps, no cell twice within a word) to one path of (row, col) cells."""
    trie = {}
    for word in words:
        node = trie
        for ch in word:
            node = node.setdefault(ch, {})
        node['$word'] = word                      # multi-character key: never equals a board letter
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0]) if board else 0
    found, path, used = {}, [], set()

    def dfs(r, c, node):
        child = node.get(board[r][c])
        if child is None:
            return
        path.append((r, c))
        used.add((r, c))
        word = child.get('$word')
        if word is not None and word not in found:
            found[word] = path.copy()
        for rr, cc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= rr < rows and 0 <= cc < cols and (rr, cc) not in used:
                dfs(rr, cc, child)
        used.discard((r, c))
        path.pop()

    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            dfs(r, c, trie)
    return found

Time complexity: building the trie is O(Ltotal)O(L_{\text{total}})O(Ltotal​); the search is O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1)O(RC \cdot 4 \cdot 3^{L-1})O(RC⋅4⋅3L−1) in the worst case for words of length up to LLL, and shared prefixes are walked once.

Space complexity: O(Ltotal)O(L_{\text{total}})O(Ltotal​) for the trie, O(L)O(L)O(L) for the path and the used set.

Recording the path costs nothing extra: it is the DFS stack. The third part, the largest set of words with disjoint cells, needs every candidate path of each word, not only the first one this drill keeps. On the board [['a','b','a','b']] with words ab and ba, the stored paths share cell (0, 1), yet ab on (0, 0)-(0, 1) and ba on (0, 3)-(0, 2) are disjoint. Collect a list of paths per word, then backtrack over those lists.

1.1.10 Build order by levels#

Asked: level not stated (1181604)

Question. You are given dependency declarations. Each is a list of strings whose first element is a component and whose remaining elements are the components it depends on, which must be built before it. Return a valid build order. At each step, every component whose dependencies are all built becomes buildable at the same time; within one such level, output components in the order their declarations appear in the input. Return ["Error"] if a dependency is never declared as a first element, or if the dependencies form a cycle. Examples:

  • [["head"], ["torso"], ["leg"]] gives ["head", "torso", "leg"].
  • [["head", "leg"], ["leg", "head"]] gives ["Error"] (a cycle).
  • [["head"], ["leg", "torso"]] gives ["Error"] (torso is never declared).
  • [["hair", "head"], ["torso"], ["leg", "torso"], ["head"]] gives ["torso", "head", "hair", "leg"].

Answer. Kahn's algorithm, one level at a time. Map each component to its declaration index; if any dependency is undeclared, return ["Error"]. Set each component's indegree to its number of distinct dependencies. Level 0 is the components with indegree 0, sorted by declaration index; to form the next level, decrement the indegree of every dependent of the current level, collect those that reach 0 and sort them by declaration index. If fewer than VVV components come out, the rest sit on or behind a cycle: return ["Error"]. O(V+E+Vlog⁡V)O(V+E+V\log V)O(V+E+VlogV) time and O(V+E)O(V+E)O(V+E) space. A single priority queue keyed by declaration index is wrong: on the fourth example it outputs torso, leg, head, hair, because leg (level 1) overtakes head (level 0). A self-dependency is a cycle; deduplicate repeated dependencies; ask what a component declared twice means.

Coding: build order by levels [READY]View exercise
python
from collections import defaultdict


def build_order(declarations):
    """Each declaration is [component, *dependencies]. Build level by level; inside a level keep the
    declaration order. ["Error"] for a dependency that is never declared or for a cycle."""
    position = {decl[0]: i for i, decl in enumerate(declarations)}
    requires = {decl[0]: set(decl[1:]) for decl in declarations}
    if any(dep not in position for deps in requires.values() for dep in deps):
        return ["Error"]
    waiting = {c: len(deps) for c, deps in requires.items()}
    users = defaultdict(list)
    for component, deps in requires.items():
        for dep in deps:
            users[dep].append(component)
    level = sorted((c for c in requires if waiting[c] == 0), key=position.get)
    order = []
    while level:
        order.extend(level)
        ready = []
        for built in level:
            for user in users[built]:
                waiting[user] -= 1
                if waiting[user] == 0:
                    ready.append(user)
        level = sorted(ready, key=position.get)
    return order if len(order) == len(requires) else ["Error"]

Time complexity: O(V+E+Vlog⁡V)O(V + E + V \log V)O(V+E+VlogV): Kahn's algorithm plus a sort of each level by declaration position.

Space complexity: O(V+E)O(V + E)O(V+E).

1.1.11 Other problems#

Closest BST value, harder variant (LeetCode 270)#

Asked: level not stated (1158688)

Question. A harder variant of LeetCode 270 (given a binary search tree and a target, return the value closest to the target) with extra constraints that the poster did not recall.

Answer. Base: walk down from the root, update the best value whenever ∣v−t∣|v-t|∣v−t∣ improves (ties to the smaller value), and go left if t<vt<vt<v, else right; O(h)O(h)O(h) time and O(1)O(1)O(1) space. Have the usual harder forms ready: the kkk closest values (LeetCode 272), with a predecessor stack and a successor stack merged like two sorted lists in O(h+k)O(h+k)O(h+k), or an in-order pass with a size-kkk deque in O(n)O(n)O(n); the floor or ceiling of ttt (largest value ≤t\le t≤t, smallest value ≥t\ge t≥t) with the same walk; and a tree with no BST guarantee, which needs a full traversal in O(n)O(n)O(n). Edge cases: an empty tree, a target outside the value range, duplicates, and overflow of ∣v−t∣|v-t|∣v−t∣ with fixed-width integers.

Single-Threaded CPU (LeetCode 1834)#

Asked: senior (1128678)

Question. LeetCode 1834: tasks[i] = [enqueueTime, processingTime]. Whenever a single CPU is idle, it starts the available task with the shortest processing time, ties going to the smaller index, and runs it to completion; if no task is available, it waits for the next one. Return the order in which the tasks are processed.

Answer. Sort the indices by enqueue time and keep a min-heap of (processing time, index). Loop with a clock TTT: push every task with enqueue time ≤T\le T≤T; if the heap is empty, jump TTT to the next enqueue time; otherwise pop, append the index and add its processing time to TTT. Each task is pushed and popped once: O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) time and O(n)O(n)O(n) space. Use 64-bit time, since the clock can reach 105⋅10910^5\cdot 10^9105⋅109, and push all tasks that share an enqueue time before choosing.

Key-value store with transactions#

Asked: level not stated (927016)

Question. Implement an in-memory key-value store that supports transactions, as plain coding: no locks, write-ahead log or isolation levels.

Answer. Support the usual API, get, set, delete, begin, commit and rollback, with nested transactions. Keep the current data in one dict and a stack of undo logs, one per open transaction; the first time a transaction changes a key, it records the key's previous value or "absent". get and set stay O(1)O(1)O(1). rollback replays the top log in O(changes)O(\text{changes})O(changes) and pops it. Committing a nested transaction merges its log into the parent's, keeping the parent's older entry for keys both touched; a top-level commit just drops the log. The alternative is a stack of overlay dicts with tombstones for deletes, where get searches from the top layer down in O(depth)O(\text{depth})O(depth). If the API also counts keys per value, keep a value-to-count map and update it on every write and every undo. Edge cases: commit or rollback with no open transaction, whether commit closes only the innermost transaction or all of them, deleting a missing key, and a key set to its current value.

Initialize a connect-3 board#

Asked: level not stated (927016)

Question. Initialize a connect-3 board. Nothing more of the statement was reported, except that filling it with two plain nested loops can produce invalid boards, which a DFS fixed. The common reading: fill an R×CR\times CR×C board with random colours so that no row or column already holds three equal cells in a row.

Answer. Fill the cells in row-major order. At (r,c)(r,c)(r,c), forbid the colour of the two cells to the left if they are equal and the colour of the two cells above if they are equal, then pick at random from the remaining colours. With 3 or more colours at most 2 are forbidden, so the fill never gets stuck: O(RC)O(RC)O(RC). With 2 colours both can be forbidden, and that is when a DFS with backtracking is needed. If the board must also allow at least one move that makes a match, test that after filling and regenerate.

Connect 4 winner#

Asked: level not stated (874270)

Question. Two players take turns dropping pieces into a Connect 4 board; determine which player is first to connect four.

Answer. Keep the board and a height per column, so a drop lands in O(1)O(1)O(1). After each drop at (r,c)(r,c)(r,c), for each of the 4 lines through it (horizontal, vertical and the two diagonals), count same-colour cells forward and backward; 1+forward+backward≥41+\text{forward}+\text{backward}\ge 41+forward+backward≥4 wins. That is O(1)O(1)O(1) per move, O(k)O(k)O(k) for connect-kkk, with O(RC)O(RC)O(RC) space; given a full move list, return the first winner and the move that won. Handle a move into a full column, a draw when the board fills, and moves after the game is over.

Mahjong hand check, then with sequences#

Asked: level not stated (886138)

Question. Two parts: check a mahjong hand, then the same check when sequences are allowed. The thread gives no more; the usual form is a hand of numbered tiles that is complete when it splits into exactly one pair plus any number of triples of equal tiles, and part 2 also accepts three consecutive numbers as a group.

Answer. Part 1: count the tiles; the hand is complete exactly when one tile value has a count ≡2(mod3)\equiv 2 \pmod 3≡2(mod3) and every other count is ≡0(mod3)\equiv 0 \pmod 3≡0(mod3) (a count of 5 is a pair plus a triple); O(n)O(n)O(n). Part 2: the hand size must be ≡2(mod3)\equiv 2 \pmod 3≡2(mod3). Try each value with count ≥2\ge 2≥2 as the pair and remove it, then scan values in increasing order: the smallest remaining value xxx, with count ccc, can only sit in triples or start sequences, so form c mod 3c \bmod 3cmod3 sequences x,x+1,x+2x,x+1,x+2x,x+1,x+2 (fail if x+1x+1x+1 or x+2x+2x+2 runs short) and ⌊c/3⌋\lfloor c/3\rfloor⌊c/3⌋ triples. Three equal sequences use the same tiles as three triples, so this greedy is exact. O(V)O(V)O(V) per pair choice for VVV tile values, O(n+V2)O(n+V^2)O(n+V2) in total. Ask about suits (sequences never cross suits) and the hand size.

Find peak#

Asked: level not stated (889847)

Question. Find a peak element; the thread does not say whether in an array (LeetCode 162) or in a matrix (LeetCode 1901).

Answer. Array: treat out-of-range neighbours as −∞-\infty−∞ and binary search; if amid<amid+1a_{mid}<a_{mid+1}amid​<amid+1​ a peak lies to the right, otherwise at midmidmid or to its left. O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn), assuming adjacent values differ. Matrix: binary search on columns; take the maximum of the middle column in O(R)O(R)O(R) and move toward a strictly larger horizontal neighbour, or stop because that cell is a peak; O(Rlog⁡C)O(R\log C)O(RlogC). With equal neighbours the array search still returns an element at least as large as both neighbours, but a strict peak may not exist at all (a constant array has none), so agree on the definition first.

Design git (object-oriented)#

Asked: level not stated (768938)

Question. An object-oriented design problem best described as "design git"; no further specification was reported.

Answer. Store objects by content hash: a blob (file content), a tree (names to blob or tree hashes) and a commit (tree hash, parent hashes, author, message, timestamp). Refs map branch names to commit hashes, and HEAD names a branch or, when detached, a commit. Operations: add stages a file in an index; commit builds a tree from the index, writes a commit whose parent is HEAD and advances the branch; branch creates a ref; checkout moves HEAD and rewrites the working files; log walks parent pointers; merge finds a merge base, a common ancestor in the commit DAG that no other common ancestor descends from (mark the ancestors of one commit by BFS, then BFS from the other; criss-cross histories can have several), then merges each file three ways and reports conflicts. Objects are immutable and deduplicated by their hash. Keep the classes small (Repository, ObjectStore, Blob, Tree, Commit, Ref) and agree on scope (single user, local only, text files) before writing code.

Analyze user website visit pattern, variant (LeetCode 1152)#

Asked: level not stated (830336)

Question. A variant of LeetCode 1152 with a very long description and many corner cases, plus one more corner case added after the code was written. The base problem: given parallel arrays username, timestamp and website, find the pattern of 3 websites, visited in that order by time but not necessarily consecutively, that the most users share; ties go to the lexicographically smallest pattern.

Answer. Group the visits by user and sort each user's visits by timestamp. For each user, generate the 3-patterns over index triples i<j<ki<j<ki<j<k into a set, so a user counts once per pattern, and add the set into a global counter. Return the pattern with the highest count, ties to the lexicographically smallest. Cost: O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) to sort plus O(∑u(mu3))O\bigl(\sum_u \binom{m_u}{3}\bigr)O(∑u​(3mu​​)) for mum_umu​ visits by user uuu. Corner cases: users with fewer than 3 visits, a site repeated inside a pattern (allowed), equal timestamps (ask how to order them), and the tie rule.

Implement two-phase commit#

Asked: level not stated (830336)

Question. Implement the two-phase commit protocol from a long written specification.

Answer. One coordinator and nnn participants. Phase 1 (prepare): the coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant durably logs its vote and answers YES, after which it is prepared and holds its locks, or NO. Phase 2 (decision): if every vote is YES, the coordinator logs COMMIT and sends COMMIT; on any NO, or a timeout while waiting for votes, it logs and sends ABORT. Participants apply the decision, release their locks and acknowledge, and the coordinator logs END after every acknowledgement. The coordinator moves through INIT, WAIT, then COMMIT or ABORT; a participant through INIT, READY, then COMMIT or ABORT. Recovery reads the log: a coordinator with no decision record aborts, and a participant in READY cannot decide alone and must learn the outcome from the coordinator or from a participant that knows it, which is why 2PC blocks if the coordinator fails after collecting the votes. Make messages idempotent and resend the decision until it is acknowledged. A commit costs 4n4n4n messages. Paxos Commit removes the blocking; three-phase commit removes it only on a synchronous network without partitions.

1.2 ML questions#

1.2.1 Transformers and LLMs#

How the Transformer works#

Asked: PhD new grad (1124594), IC6 (principal) (995525), level not stated (1123499, 1125433, 1124873, 1050390)

Question. Explain how the Transformer works: the overall architecture and the role of each layer, the attention computation, and what the query, key and value (Q, K, V) are.

Answer. Each token embedding x∈Rdx \in \mathbb{R}^{d}x∈Rd is projected three ways: a query q=xWQq = xW_Qq=xWQ​ (what this token is looking for), a key k=xWKk = xW_Kk=xWK​ (what it offers to be matched on) and a value v=xWVv = xW_Vv=xWV​ (the content it passes on). Stacking the tokens into matrices gives

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤dk+M)V\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)VAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​+M)V

Row iii of the softmax is a distribution over positions jjj that says how much token iii reads from token jjj, and the output is the matching weighted sum of values. MMM is 000 or −∞-\infty−∞ per entry (causal or padding mask). If the components of qqq and kkk are independent with zero mean and unit variance, q⊤kq^{\top}kq⊤k has variance dkd_kdk​, so dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ keeps the logits at unit variance and the softmax out of saturation. Multi-head attention runs hhh heads of width dk=d/hd_k = d/hdk​=d/h, each with its own projections, concatenates them and mixes them with WOW_OWO​, so different heads can track different relations at about the same cost as one full-width head.

A block wraps attention and a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN) in residual connections and layer normalization. In the pre-LN form used by modern LLMs:

h=x+MHA(LN(x)),y=h+FFN(LN(h)),FFN(h)=ϕ(hW1) W2h = x + \mathrm{MHA}\bigl(\mathrm{LN}(x)\bigr), \qquad y = h + \mathrm{FFN}\bigl(\mathrm{LN}(h)\bigr), \qquad \mathrm{FFN}(h) = \phi(hW_1)\,W_2h=x+MHA(LN(x)),y=h+FFN(LN(h)),FFN(h)=ϕ(hW1​)W2​

The original paper used post-LN, LN(x+sublayer(x))\mathrm{LN}(x + \mathrm{sublayer}(x))LN(x+sublayer(x)), with ϕ=ReLU\phi = \mathrm{ReLU}ϕ=ReLU and dff=4dd_{ff} = 4ddff​=4d; current models use GELU or SwiGLU and often RMSNorm. Attention is permutation-invariant, so position must be injected (see positional encodings below). Encoder blocks use bidirectional self-attention. Decoder blocks use causally masked self-attention, and in an encoder-decoder model they add cross-attention whose queries come from the decoder and whose keys and values come from the encoder output. A final linear layer and softmax over the vocabulary give next-token probabilities. Per layer, the attention scores cost O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) and the projections and FFN cost O(nd2)O(nd^2)O(nd2).

Transformers compared with RNNs and LSTMs#

Asked: level not stated (1123499)

Question. What are the advantages of the Transformer over RNNs and LSTMs?

Answer.

RNNs process tokens sequentially, maintaining a hidden state that summarizes previous inputs. However, they struggle with long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients and cannot parallelize computation across time steps.

LSTMs improve RNNs by introducing a cell state and input, forget, and output gates. These mechanisms help preserve information and improve gradient flow over longer sequences, but computation remains sequential.

Transformers replace recurrence with self-attention, enabling parallel processing during training and direct interactions between tokens. This significantly improves scalability and long-range dependency modeling. However, standard self-attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length, and autoregressive inference requires a growing KV cache.

In more detail:

  • Parallel training: all positions are computed at once with matrix multiplications, while an RNN needs nnn sequential steps. This suits GPUs and is what lets Transformers scale to large models and data.
  • Short paths: any two tokens interact in one attention step (path length O(1)O(1)O(1) instead of O(n)O(n)O(n)), so long-range dependencies are easier to learn and gradients do not pass through nnn multiplied Jacobians.
  • Input-dependent weighting: attention weights are computed from the content, so the model chooses what to read at each position.
  • Costs: O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) time and memory in sequence length; no built-in notion of order, so positions must be encoded; and autoregressive decoding needs a KV cache that grows with length, while an RNN carries a fixed-size state with O(1)O(1)O(1) memory per step.
What prevents vanishing gradients in a Transformer#

Asked: level not stated (1123499)

Question. What in the Transformer prevents vanishing gradients?

Answer.

  • Residual connections: with xl+1=xl+Fl(xl)x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(x_l)xl+1​=xl​+Fl​(xl​), the Jacobian is ∂xl+1/∂xl=I+∂Fl/∂xl\partial x_{l+1} / \partial x_l = I + \partial F_l / \partial x_l∂xl+1​/∂xl​=I+∂Fl​/∂xl​, so the gradient always has an identity path through the whole depth.
  • Layer normalization keeps activation scales stable. Pre-LN leaves the residual stream itself un-normalized, so the identity path stays clean and training is stable without a long warmup; post-LN needs warmup.
  • The 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ scaling keeps the softmax away from saturation, where its gradient goes to zero.
  • Non-saturating activations (ReLU, GELU) in the FFN.
  • Along the sequence, attention connects positions directly, avoiding the long products of Jacobians of backpropagation through time.
  • Training details: initialization that scales the residual-branch output weights down with depth (GPT-2 uses 1/N1/\sqrt{N}1/N​ for NNN residual layers), learning-rate warmup and gradient clipping.
Attention complexity and where the parameters are#

Asked: level not stated (1123499)

Question. What is the time complexity of an attention block, and is it quadratic? Which part of the Transformer has the most parameters?

Answer. Take one layer with sequence length nnn, width ddd and dff=4dd_{ff} = 4ddff​=4d. The multiply-accumulates are about 4nd24nd^24nd2 for the Q, K, V and output projections, 2n2d2n^2 d2n2d for QK⊤QK^{\top}QK⊤ and the weighted sum of VVV, and 8nd28nd^28nd2 for the FFN:

cost per layer≈12nd2+2n2d\text{cost per layer} \approx 12nd^2 + 2n^2 dcost per layer≈12nd2+2n2d

So attention is quadratic in nnn, but the quadratic term dominates only when n>6dn > 6dn>6d; for shorter sequences the projections and FFN dominate. The score matrix also needs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) memory per head unless a fused kernel such as FlashAttention avoids materializing it. With a KV cache, generating one token costs, per layer, O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) for attention plus O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) for the dense layers.

Parameters per layer: attention has WQ,WK,WV,WOW_Q, W_K, W_V, W_OWQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​, which is 4d24d^24d2; the FFN has W1∈Rd×4dW_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 4d}W1​∈Rd×4d and W2∈R4d×dW_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{4d \times d}W2​∈R4d×d, which is 8d28d^28d2. In the standard configuration the FFN therefore holds about two-thirds of each block. Grouped-query attention shrinks the attention share further, and SwiGLU with dff≈83dd_{ff} \approx \tfrac{8}{3}ddff​≈38​d uses three matrices and keeps the FFN at about 8d28d^28d2. Outside the blocks, the token embedding table (∣V∣⋅d\lvert \mathcal{V} \rvert \cdot d∣V∣⋅d for vocabulary V\mathcal{V}V) can be the largest single matrix in small models: about 39M of GPT-2 small's 124M parameters. The split depends on the configuration; for the standard one the answer is the FFN.

Making self-attention faster#

Asked: PhD new grad (1124594), level not stated (1123499, 1125433)

Question. How do you make self-attention faster? What are linear and sparse self-attention? Which Transformer optimizations, such as FlashAttention, do you know?

Answer. Separate exact kernel-level speedups from changes to the attention function itself.

  1. Exact, IO-aware kernels. FlashAttention computes exact attention without writing the n×nn \times nn×n score matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). It tiles QQQ, KKK and VVV into on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax: each query row keeps a running max mmm, normalizer ℓ\ellℓ and unnormalized output ooo, and each new block of scores sjs_jsj​ with values vjv_jvj​ updates them as

    m′=max⁡(m,max⁡jsj),ℓ′=em−m′ ℓ+∑jesj−m′,o′=em−m′ o+∑jesj−m′ vjm' = \max\bigl(m, \max_j s_j\bigr), \qquad \ell' = e^{m - m'}\,\ell + \sum_j e^{s_j - m'}, \qquad o' = e^{m - m'}\, o + \sum_j e^{s_j - m'}\, v_jm′=max(m,jmax​sj​),ℓ′=em−m′ℓ+j∑​esj​−m′,o′=em−m′o+j∑​esj​−m′vj​

    with the final output o/ℓo / \ello/ℓ. The backward pass recomputes the scores from the saved row statistics instead of storing them. FLOPs stay O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d), but extra memory falls from O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) to O(n)O(n)O(n) and HBM traffic drops sharply, which is where the speedup comes from. It is a kernel optimization, not an architectural change: the outputs match standard attention up to floating-point error. FlashAttention-2 cuts the non-matmul work and also parallelizes over the sequence dimension; FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper GPUs with asynchronous, warp-specialized pipelines (TMA), overlaps the softmax with the matmuls and adds FP8.

  2. Sparse attention. Each query attends to a subset of keys: a local window of width www, a few global tokens, or strided or random positions (Sparse Transformer, Longformer, BigBird). The cost drops from O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) to O(nwd)O(nwd)O(nwd). Sliding-window attention is also used in LLMs such as Mistral.

  3. Linear attention. Replace exp⁡(q⊤k)\exp(q^{\top}k)exp(q⊤k) with a feature map ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k)\phi(q)^{\top}\phi(k)ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k) and reassociate the product:

    oi=ϕ(qi)⊤Sϕ(qi)⊤z,S=∑jϕ(kj) vj⊤,z=∑jϕ(kj)o_i = \frac{\phi(q_i)^{\top} S}{\phi(q_i)^{\top} z}, \qquad S = \sum_j \phi(k_j)\, v_j^{\top}, \qquad z = \sum_j \phi(k_j)oi​=ϕ(qi​)⊤zϕ(qi​)⊤S​,S=j∑​ϕ(kj​)vj⊤​,z=j∑​ϕ(kj​)

    All queries share S∈Rr×dvS \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_v}S∈Rr×dv​ and z∈Rrz \in \mathbb{R}^{r}z∈Rr, so the cost is O(nrdv)O(n r d_v)O(nrdv​), linear in nnn. The causal version keeps running prefix sums of SSS and zzz and behaves like an RNN with a matrix-valued state. Examples are the linear Transformer (ϕ(x)=elu(x)+1\phi(x) = \mathrm{elu}(x) + 1ϕ(x)=elu(x)+1) and Performer (random features that approximate the softmax kernel). There is usually some quality loss compared with softmax attention.

  4. Other approximations of the softmax matrix: low-rank projection of KKK and VVV along the sequence to a fixed length (Linformer), and hashing similar queries and keys into buckets so attention is computed within buckets (Reformer).

  5. Inference-side: a KV cache so past keys and values are not recomputed, multi-query or grouped-query attention to shrink that cache and its memory bandwidth, and PagedAttention to manage cache memory in batched serving.

Original Transformer, BERT, T5, and GPT#

Asked: GPT/BERT pre-training and architecture — PhD new grad (1124594); T5/GPT comparison — level not stated (1050390). These two reported topics are combined below; the original Transformer is added as explanatory context.

Question. Compare the original Transformer, BERT, T5 and GPT: architecture, attention visibility, training targets, loss functions, and how they are used after training.

Answer. Separate architecture from training objective. An encoder-decoder is a structure, not a particular pre-training task. Here, "original Transformer" means the 2017 translation model, BERT and T5 mean their original versions, and GPT means a causal decoder-only language model with GPT-2 as the concrete implementation example. Do not assume that every later model uses the same normalization or position scheme.

Side-by-side structure and training.

DimensionOriginal TransformerBERTT5GPT / GPT-2
Main structureEncoder + decoderEncoder onlyEncoder + decoderDecoder-only stack
Self-attention visibilityBidirectional encoder; causal decoderBidirectional over the corrupted inputBidirectional encoder; causal decoderCausal over one token stream
Cross-attentionDecoder reads encoder outputNoneDecoder reads encoder outputNone in the standard GPT-2 block
Training data and taskPaired source/target translations; supervisedUnlabeled text; masked tokens + sentence-pair objectiveUnlabeled text; recover removed spansUnlabeled text; predict the next token
Token-loss positionsTarget-language positionsSelected token positionsSerialized missing spans and sentinelsNext-token targets across the sequence
Typical task interfaceSource text → target textAdd a classification, tagging or span headText → text, including labels written as textPrompt → continuation; task-specific fine-tuning is also possible
Position informationSinusoidal absolute positions in the main configurationLearned absolute positions + segment embeddingsLearned bucketed relative attention biasLearned absolute positions in GPT-2
Norm / FFN activationPost-LN / ReLUPost-LN / GELUPre-norm, RMS-style / ReLUPre-LN + final LN / GELU

These are canonical configurations, not performance rankings. Architecture and objective are described in the Transformer paper, BERT paper, T5 paper, and GPT-2 report. Implementation details can be checked in the original BERT code and GPT-2 code.

Attention masks and tensor flow.

Let BBB be batch size, LLL input length, TTT output length, ddd hidden width, hhh the number of heads, dh=d/hd_h=d/hdh​=d/h, and VVV vocabulary size. Ignoring padding, bidirectional self-attention permits every input position; causal self-attention uses

Mijcausal={0,j≤i,−∞,j>i.M_{ij}^{\mathrm{causal}}= \begin{cases} 0,&j\le i,\\ -\infty,&j>i. \end{cases}Mijcausal​={0,−∞,​j≤i,j>i.​

This mask is added to attention logits before softmax. In an encoder-decoder, the flow is

H=Encoder⁡(x)∈RB×L×d,D=Decoder⁡(yshifted,H)∈RB×T×d,Z=DWvocab+b∈RB×T×V.H=\operatorname{Encoder}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times d},\qquad D=\operatorname{Decoder}(y_{\mathrm{shifted}},H)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d},\qquad Z=DW_{\mathrm{vocab}}+b\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times V}.H=Encoder(x)∈RB×L×d,D=Decoder(yshifted​,H)∈RB×T×d,Z=DWvocab​+b∈RB×T×V.

Here yshifted=[BOS,y1,…,yT−1]y_{\mathrm{shifted}}=[\mathrm{BOS},y_1,\ldots,y_{T-1}]yshifted​=[BOS,y1​,…,yT−1​], and softmax⁡(Zt)\operatorname{softmax}(Z_t)softmax(Zt​) predicts yty_tyt​. In one cross-attention head, queries come from the current decoder states SSS, while keys and values come from the encoder:

Q=SWQ∈RB×T×dh,K=HWK, Venc=HWV∈RB×L×dh,QK⊤∈RB×T×L.Q=SW_Q\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d_h},\quad K=HW_K,\ V_{\mathrm{enc}}=HW_V\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times d_h},\quad QK^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times L}.Q=SWQ​∈RB×T×dh​,K=HWK​, Venc​=HWV​∈RB×L×dh​,QK⊤∈RB×T×L.

The transpose is over the final two dimensions. Each output position can read all valid input positions. BERT has only the encoder path; GPT has a causal stream and vocabulary head, not this encoder/cross-attention path. Autoregressive does not imply cross-attention.

1. Original Transformer — supervised conditional generation.

Given a source sentence xxx and its translation yyy, learn

pθ(y∣x)=∏t=1Tpθ(yt∣y<t,x),Ltranslation=−∑t=1Tlog⁡pθ(yt∣y<t,x).p_\theta(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(y_t\mid y_{<t},x),\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{translation}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(y_t\mid y_{<t},x).pθ​(y∣x)=t=1∏T​pθ​(yt​∣y<t​,x),Ltranslation​=−t=1∑T​logpθ​(yt​∣y<t​,x).

The decoder receives the shifted ground-truth translation during training: teacher forcing. This is paired translation training, not generic next-token pre-training on unlabeled text. The formula shows the basic token NLL; the original paper additionally uses label smoothing.

2. BERT — predict selected tokens using both sides.

Let M\mathcal{M}M contain the selected positions and x~\tilde xx~ be the corrupted input:

LMLM=−∑i∈Mlog⁡pθ(xi∣x~),LBERT=LMLM+LNSP.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLM}}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}\log p_\theta(x_i\mid\tilde x),\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BERT}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLM}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NSP}}.LMLM​=−i∈M∑​logpθ​(xi​∣x~),LBERT​=LMLM​+LNSP​.

Original BERT selects 15% of tokens: 80% of those become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% remain unchanged. All selected positions contribute to MLM, not only literal [MASK] positions. NSP is a binary next-sentence classification loss from [CLS]. At fine-tuning, a task head can use hCLSh_{\mathrm{CLS}}hCLS​ or individual token states. This is not native left-to-right generation. BERT pre-training details.

3. T5 — encode corrupted text, autoregressively generate missing spans.

Replace each removed span with a distinct sentinel to form x~\tilde xx~. Serialize the removed spans and their sentinel markers into a target sequence zzz:

LT5=−∑t=1∣z∣log⁡pθ(zt∣z<t,x~).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{T5}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{|z|}\log p_\theta(z_t\mid z_{<t},\tilde x).LT5​=−t=1∑∣z∣​logpθ​(zt​∣z<t​,x~).

T5 corrupts about 15% of tokens with mean span length 3. Its decoder predicts missing spans plus markers, not the entire original input. The encoder reads the corrupted input bidirectionally; the decoder remains causal. Fine-tuning keeps a text-to-text interface, such as a translation prefix or generating a class name. T5 span-corruption objective.

4. GPT — autoregressive next-token pre-training.

pθ(x)=∏t=1Lpθ(xt∣x<t),LGPT=−∑t=1Llog⁡pθ(xt∣x<t).p_\theta(x)=\prod_{t=1}^{L}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}),\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GPT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{L}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).pθ​(x)=t=1∏L​pθ​(xt​∣x<t​),LGPT​=−t=1∑L​logpθ​(xt​∣x<t​).

Input and continuation occupy one causal stream. There is no separate bidirectional encoder. At generation time, append a generated token and predict the next one. The GPT-2 report uses this language-model objective; prompting is a task interface, not a different pre-training loss.

One toy sentence, three learning targets. Words below stand for tokens; actual tokenizers may split them differently. These toy examples illustrate the objectives, not their real corruption percentages.

text
Original text: I enjoy playing games

BERT input:   I [MASK] playing games
MLM target:   enjoy at the selected position

T5 input:     I <extra_id_0> games
T5 target:    <extra_id_0> enjoy playing <extra_id_1> EOS

GPT input:    BOS I enjoy playing
GPT targets:  I   enjoy playing games
              Each position predicts the next token.

Training parallelism versus generation. Teacher-forced original Transformer, T5, and GPT can compute all supervised decoder positions in parallel because the shifted true tokens are supplied and a causal mask prevents future-token leakage. At inference, they must generate successive tokens from their own prefixes. BERT predicts its selected positions in parallel without defining this left-to-right generation process.

Norm placement is a separate design choice. For a sublayer FFF, post-LN is x′=LN⁡(x+F(x))x'=\operatorname{LN}(x+F(x))x′=LN(x+F(x)); pre-LN is x′=x+F(Norm⁡(x))x'=x+F(\operatorname{Norm}(x))x′=x+F(Norm(x)). Do not confuse pre/post-normalization with bidirectional/causal masking: the former controls the residual computation; the latter controls which tokens can communicate.

Positional encodings#

Asked: PhD new grad (1124594)

Question. What kinds of positional encoding are there, and what are the pros and cons of each?

Answer.

TypeIdeaProsCons
Sinusoidal, absolute (original Transformer)Add PE(p,2i)=sin⁡(p/100002i/d)PE_{(p,2i)} = \sin(p / 10000^{2i/d})PE(p,2i)​=sin(p/100002i/d) and PE(p,2i+1)=cos⁡(p/100002i/d)PE_{(p,2i+1)} = \cos(p / 10000^{2i/d})PE(p,2i+1)​=cos(p/100002i/d) to the inputNo parameters; defined for any length; a fixed offset is a linear map of the encodingExtrapolates poorly beyond trained lengths in practice; position is mixed into the content vector
Learned, absolute (BERT, GPT-2)One trainable vector per position, added to the inputSimple and flexibleHard maximum length; nothing learned for unseen positions
Relative (Shaw et al.; T5 bias)A learned embedding or scalar bias per clipped or bucketed offset i−ji - ji−j, applied inside attentionTranslation-invariant; generalizes better across lengthsExtra work inside every attention layer; buckets are coarse at long range
RoPE (LLaMA and most current LLMs)Rotate each 2-D pair of qqq and kkk at position mmm by angle mθim\theta_imθi​, θi=10000−2i/d\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}θi​=10000−2i/d, so ⟨Rmq,Rnk⟩\langle R_m q, R_n k \rangle⟨Rm​q,Rn​k⟩ depends on position only through n−mn - mn−mRelative, no parameters, applied only to qqq and kkk, so it works with the KV cache and fused kernels; context can be extended with position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling or YaRNDegrades beyond the trained length without such scaling
ALiBiAdd −mh(i−j)-m_h (i - j)−mh​(i−j) to the logit of query iii and key j≤ij \le ij≤i, with a fixed slope mhm_hmh​ per headNo parameters; extrapolates to longer inputsStrong recency bias can hurt use of distant tokens; less common in recent LLMs

1.2.2 Distributed training#

Distributed training, tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism#

Asked: PhD new grad (1124594)

Question. What kinds of distributed training are there? How does tensor parallelism (TP) work in detail? What are the drawbacks of pipeline parallelism (PP), and how do you mitigate them?

Answer.

  • Data parallelism (DP). Each GPU holds a full replica and processes its own micro-batch, and the gradients are averaged with an all-reduce every step, overlapped with the backward pass by bucketing. A ring all-reduce moves about 2(N−1)/N2(N-1)/N2(N−1)/N times the gradient size per GPU, nearly independent of NNN. Mixed-precision Adam needs about 16Ψ16\Psi16Ψ bytes for Ψ\PsiΨ parameters (fp16 weights and gradients plus fp32 master weights and two moments), so ZeRO and FSDP shard the optimizer states (stage 1), the gradients (stage 2) and the parameters (stage 3), gathering parameters just in time; stage 3 costs about 1.5 times the communication of plain DP.

  • Tensor parallelism (TP, Megatron-LM). Split the weight matrices inside each layer across ttt GPUs. For the FFN Z=GeLU(XA) BZ = \mathrm{GeLU}(XA)\,BZ=GeLU(XA)B, split A=[A1,…,At]A = [A_1, \dots, A_t]A=[A1​,…,At​] by columns, so GPU iii computes Yi=GeLU(XAi)Y_i = \mathrm{GeLU}(XA_i)Yi​=GeLU(XAi​) locally (GeLU is elementwise, so no communication is needed); split BBB by rows, so GPU iii computes YiBiY_i B_iYi​Bi​; then one all-reduce gives Z=∑iYiBiZ = \sum_i Y_i B_iZ=∑i​Yi​Bi​. Attention is split by heads: WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​ are column-parallel, so each GPU computes whole heads, and WOW_OWO​ is row-parallel, followed by one all-reduce. That is two all-reduces per layer in the forward pass and two in the backward pass, all on the critical path, so TP is kept inside a node on NVLink (typically t≤8t \le 8t≤8). The embedding and output layers are split along the vocabulary. Sequence parallelism replaces each all-reduce with a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather and shards the LayerNorm and dropout activations along the sequence, which cuts activation memory.

  • Pipeline parallelism (PP). Put consecutive layers on ppp stages and stream mmm micro-batches through them. Drawbacks:

    • the bubble: stages sit idle while the pipeline fills and drains, a fraction (p−1)/(m+p−1)(p-1)/(m+p-1)(p−1)/(m+p−1) of the time with a GPipe schedule;
    • activation memory for all micro-batches in flight;
    • load imbalance between stages (the embedding and output head make the first and last stages heavier);
    • point-to-point latency between stages, and a large global batch, since m≫pm \gg pm≫p is needed, which can affect convergence.

    Mitigations:

    • many more micro-batches than stages;
    • 1F1B scheduling, which keeps the GPipe bubble but caps in-flight activations at about ppp micro-batches;
    • interleaved virtual stages: vvv model chunks per GPU shrink the bubble by about a factor vvv, at the cost of more communication;
    • zero-bubble schedules, which split the backward pass into input-gradient and weight-gradient parts and use the weight-gradient work to fill the bubble;
    • activation recomputation, and balancing layers across stages.

  • Others. Context (sequence) parallelism, such as ring attention, splits long sequences across GPUs; expert parallelism places MoE experts on different GPUs and routes tokens with all-to-all. Large runs combine them as 3-D parallelism: TP within a node, PP across nodes and DP or FSDP on top.

1.2.3 Recommender systems and two-tower models#

Two-tower models#

Asked: senior (1128678), IC6 (principal) (995525)

Question. Explain two-tower models and answer follow-up questions on them.

Answer. A user tower u=fθ(user features, history, context)u = f_\theta(\text{user features, history, context})u=fθ​(user features, history, context) and an item tower vi=gϕ(item ID, genre, creator, statistics, text)v_i = g_\phi(\text{item ID, genre, creator, statistics, text})vi​=gϕ​(item ID, genre, creator, statistics, text), each an MLP over embeddings, output L2-normalized vectors, and the score is s(u,i)=⟨u,vi⟩/τs(u,i) = \langle u, v_i \rangle / \taus(u,i)=⟨u,vi​⟩/τ with temperature τ\tauτ. The towers meet only at the final dot product, which is what makes retrieval over millions of items cheap. Train with a sampled softmax over in-batch negatives. In-batch negatives are sampled roughly in proportion to item popularity Q(j)Q(j)Q(j), which would over-penalize popular items, so subtract log⁡Q(j)\log Q(j)logQ(j) from every logit (logQ correction):

L=−log⁡exp⁡(s(u,i+)−log⁡Q(i+))∑j∈N∪{i+}exp⁡(s(u,j)−log⁡Q(j))\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp\bigl(s(u,i^+) - \log Q(i^+)\bigr)}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N} \cup \lbrace i^+ \rbrace} \exp\bigl(s(u,j) - \log Q(j)\bigr)}L=−log∑j∈N∪{i+}​exp(s(u,j)−logQ(j))exp(s(u,i+)−logQ(i+))​

Mix in uniformly sampled negatives from the whole corpus, and add hard negatives (shown but not played) with care, since some are false negatives. At serving time, precompute item vectors into an approximate nearest-neighbor index (HNSW, IVF-PQ, ScaNN), compute the user vector per request and take the top KKK by inner product in milliseconds. Refresh the index as items and the model change, and keep both towers on the same model version. Limitations and typical follow-ups: there are no early user-item feature crosses, so it is a retrieval model and a heavier ranker re-scores its output; new items get vectors from content features in the item tower rather than an untrained ID embedding; popular items dominate without logQ correction; evaluate it with Recall@K. Matrix factorization is the special case where both towers are ID embeddings only.

Optimizing a game recommender for play time#

Asked: IC6 (principal) (995525)

Question. In an ML design question on in-session game recommendation for the home page, the objective discussed was play time. How do you model and optimize for play time?

Answer. Two standard formulations:

  1. Decompose. Expected play time per impression is E[T]=P(play)⋅E[T∣play]\mathbb{E}[T] = P(\text{play}) \cdot \mathbb{E}[T \mid \text{play}]E[T]=P(play)⋅E[T∣play]. Train a BCE head for P(play)P(\text{play})P(play) on all impressions and a regression head for E[T∣play]\mathbb{E}[T \mid \text{play}]E[T∣play] on played impressions only (Huber loss, or MSE on log⁡(1+T)\log(1+T)log(1+T), because the tail is heavy), and rank by the product or by a weighted blend with other heads such as next-day return.

  2. Weighted logistic regression. Train a classifier in which each positive is weighted by its play time TiT_iTi​ and each negative by 1. With NNN impressions of which kkk were played, the learned odds are

    ez≈∑iTiN−k=E[T]1−P(play)≈E[T](1+P(play))e^{z} \approx \frac{\sum_i T_i}{N - k} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[T]}{1 - P(\text{play})} \approx \mathbb{E}[T]\bigl(1 + P(\text{play})\bigr)ez≈N−k∑i​Ti​​=1−P(play)E[T]​≈E[T](1+P(play))

    so serving eze^{z}ez ranks by expected play time when the play rate is small.

Caveats: raw play time favors long-session genres and idle (AFK) sessions, so cap it, drop idle time or normalize per genre; it is known only when the session ends, so labels are delayed; and maximizing it alone can conflict with satisfaction and retention, so guard it with return rate and tune the blend weights online.

Home-page recommendation compared with an ads system#

Asked: principal (1132251)

Question. While designing YouTube's home-page recommendations, the candidate, whose background was ads, was challenged on how the home-page problem differs from an ads system as a business problem. How do they differ?

Answer.

  • Objective: ads maximize revenue under advertiser constraints and rank by expected value, roughly eCPM∝bid×pCTR\text{eCPM} \propto \text{bid} \times \text{pCTR}eCPM∝bid×pCTR (times pCVR for conversion bids), inside an auction with budgets, pacing and reserve prices, while user experience acts as a constraint. A home feed has no bid; it optimizes user engagement and long-term satisfaction (watch time, return visits), plus ecosystem goals such as creator exposure.
  • Calibration: essential in ads, because the predicted probability sets the price. In a feed the ordering matters most, although blending several objectives still needs scores on comparable scales.
  • Unit of evaluation: ads are judged slot by slot with few slots; a home page is judged as a whole page (diversity, freshness, dedup across rows, coverage) with many slots.
  • Labels: ads use clicks and conversions with delays and attribution problems; a feed uses watch time, likes and surveys, with long-term effects that need holdouts to measure.
  • Inventory: ad candidates are limited by targeting and budgets; a feed can show any content and needs exploration for new items and creators.
  • Shared: a retrieval-then-ranking funnel, position bias and feedback loops.

1.2.4 Features and training data#

Feature selection and processing for a game recommender#

Asked: PhD new grad (1161498)

Question. For recommending games to users, which features would you select and how would you process them?

Answer. Features, grouped by source:

  • user: coarse demographics, locale, language, device, account age;
  • user history: the last NNN games played, time-decayed play counts and play time per genre;
  • game: ID, genre, creator, age, average session length, concurrent players, rating, historical CTR and play rate;
  • context: time of day, day of week, platform;
  • social: friends currently playing and friends' recent games;
  • crosses: user-genre and user-creator affinity, and whether the user played this game before.

Processing:

  • Numeric: clip outliers, log-transform heavy-tailed counts, then standardize or bucketize.
  • Rates: smooth them toward a prior, for example CTR^=(clicks+α)/(impressions+α+β)\widehat{\text{CTR}} = (\text{clicks} + \alpha) / (\text{impressions} + \alpha + \beta)CTR=(clicks+α)/(impressions+α+β), so games with few impressions do not get extreme values.
  • Categorical: embeddings or hashing (see the next question).
  • Sequences: mean-pool or attend over the embeddings of recent games.
  • Missing values: an explicit indicator or default value.
  • Point in time: compute every feature as of the impression time.

Select features with ablations and importance scores, and keep only those available online within the latency budget.

Categorical features#

Asked: senior (1147380)

Question. How do you usually handle categorical features?

Answer.

  • Low cardinality: one-hot encoding.
  • High cardinality: learned embeddings in a DNN, or the hashing trick into a fixed number of buckets, with several hash functions to reduce collisions.
  • Target (mean) encoding works well for tree models, but compute it out of fold and smooth it toward the global mean, or it leaks the label.
  • Map rare and unseen values to an out-of-vocabulary bucket.
  • Combine fields with crosses (hashed pairs, or a learned cross layer as in DCN).
  • LightGBM and CatBoost handle categorical features natively; CatBoost uses ordered target statistics to avoid leakage.
Long-tail ID features#

Asked: senior (1147380, 1177250)

Question. An ID feature has a long-tail distribution. How do you handle it, and how do you handle the long tail in a game recommender's features and model in general?

Answer. There are two problems.

  1. Sparse embeddings for rare IDs.
    • Send IDs below a frequency threshold to a shared or hashed bucket, and use multiple hashes or quotient-remainder embeddings to limit collisions.
    • Add side features (genre, creator, tags) so tail items borrow strength from their attributes.
    • Give rare IDs smaller embeddings, or regularize them more strongly in proportion to their rarity.
  2. Popularity bias in training and exposure.
    • In retrieval, use logQ correction and popularity-aware negative sampling.
    • Add a content-based retrieval source for tail items.
    • Add exposure or diversity constraints in re-ranking, and reserve exploration slots.

Evaluate head and tail slices separately, because an overall metric can rise while tail quality falls.

Processing user interaction data#

Asked: senior (1128678)

Question. How do you process user interaction data?

Answer.

  • Labels: join impression logs to clicks and plays. A game that was shown and played is a positive, one shown and skipped is a negative, and games never shown can only be sampled negatives (absence is not dislike).
  • Cleaning: require a minimum play time so accidental clicks do not count as positives, and remove bots, duplicates and test traffic.
  • Grouping: sessionize events and aggregate repeated actions.
  • Position bias: train with position as a feature and set it to a constant at serving time, or weight examples by inverse propensity.
  • Behavior features: sequences such as the last NNN games, and time-decayed counts.
  • Leakage: split train and test by time, and join each feature as of its event's timestamp.
  • Heavy users: cap events per user so they do not dominate the loss.
Building training samples#

Asked: PhD new grad (1161498)

Question. For recommending games to users, how do you build the training samples?

Answer.

  • Unit: one example per impression (user, game, context, timestamp), with features as of that timestamp.

  • Labels: outcomes inside a fixed window after the impression, waiting until the window closes before training.

  • Ranking: learns from shown-and-not-played negatives.

  • Retrieval: needs sampled negatives (in-batch, random from the corpus, and some hard negatives).
